records.title: Cardiometabolic vulnerability and incident frailty across three aging cohorts: a multicohort longitudinal study of HRS, ELSA, and CHARLS
records.abstract: Cardiometabolic dysfunction is linked to frailty, but whether a fixed-weight biomarker score developed for one functional aging outcome retains an association with incident frailty without re-estimating its weights is unknown. We evaluated the systolic blood pressure–HDL–A1c–CRP (SHAC) index, originally developed for incident mobility limitation, across three aging cohorts.  We analyzed adults aged ≥ 65 years from HRS, ELSA, and CHARLS. Participant-specific baseline was the first eligible assessment with complete SHAC biomarkers and a valid frailty index (FI); participants frail at baseline were excluded. Incident frailty was defined as FI ≥ 0.25. Cohort-specific Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) per 1-SD higher SHAC using the original fixed weights and cohort-internal standardization, and fully adjusted estimates were pooled by random-effects meta-analysis. Sensitivity analyses addressed exposure scaling, baseline FI, outcome timing, missingness and selection, competing mortality, and longitudinally updated SHAC.  Fully adjusted analyses included 6,965 HRS participants with 3,334 events, 4,150 ELSA participants with 1,192 events, and 1,473 CHARLS participants with 476 events. HRs (95% CIs) were 1.12 (1.08–1.16), 1.21 (1.14–1.29), and 1.19 (1.08–1.30), respectively. The pooled HR was 1.16 (1.10–1.23; I²=65.9%). Adjustment for baseline FI attenuated the associations to 1.05 (1.01–1.09), 1.13 (1.06–1.20), and 1.12 (1.02–1.23). Fixed ELSA development-reference scaling also retained positive associations. Findings were broadly similar across other sensitivity analyses. HbA1c was the individual biomarker most consistently associated with incident frailty. Adding SHAC produced small increases in apparent discrimination, but SHAC did not clearly outperform HbA1c alone.  Fixed-weight SHAC was positively associated with subsequent observed frailty across HRS, ELSA, and CHARLS. These findings support further study of the previously specified SHAC weight structure as a marker of cardiometabolic vulnerability in functional aging. Cohort-dependent scaling, baseline-FI attenuation, selection, heterogeneity, and modest discrimination limit stronger claims regarding universal score transportability or clinical prediction.

records.title: Factors associated with family caregivers’ attitudes toward deprescribing in long-term care facilities: a cross-sectional study in South Korea
records.abstract: Deprescribing has emerged as an important strategy for addressing polypharmacy among older adults in long-term care facilities (LTCFs). Family caregivers often play a key role in medication-related decision-making, yet factors associated with caregivers’ attitudes toward deprescribing remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to identify the factors associated with caregivers’ attitudes toward deprescribing among residents of LTCFs in South Korea.  A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 973 family caregivers of residents in LTCFs. Attitudes toward deprescribing were assessed using the Korean version of the revised Patients’ Attitudes Towards Deprescribing questionnaire (K-rPATD). Multiple linear regression models examined the associations of 16 measured predictors, represented by 18 regression terms, with four K-rPATD subscale scores and two global items, entered simultaneously. Unadjusted and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted p values were computed for all 108 coefficients.  Of the 973 caregivers included, 56.0% were male, 88.0% had a college education or higher, and 73.0% reported dual-track prescriptions. Among the K-rPATD subscales, involvement showed the highest mean score (3.63 ± 0.61), followed by burden (3.61 ± 0.72) and concerns about stopping (3.33 ± 0.64), whereas the reverse-scored appropriateness subscale had the lowest mean (2.52 ± 0.68). Residents took an average of 5.6 ± 3.5 medications, and 16.3% had experienced adverse drug events. After FDR correction, eight associations remained significant: adverse drug events with higher burden and concerns about stopping and lower appropriateness; medication cost with higher burden and concerns about stopping; number of medications with higher burden; and number of chronic conditions with higher concerns about stopping and involvement. All other nominally significant associations did not survive FDR correction and are considered exploratory.  After correction for multiple comparisons, family caregivers’ attitudes toward deprescribing were associated with the resident’s medication-related circumstances — adverse drug events, medication cost, number of medications, and number of chronic conditions — rather than with caregivers’ own sociodemographic characteristics. These cross-sectional findings are hypothesis-generating, but they help identify the family caregivers with whom deprescribing is most likely to be a relevant topic of discussion.

records.title: Effects of an Online Training Program on Quality of Life and Caregiver Burden in Dementia Informal Caregivers
records.abstract: Informal caregivers of people living with dementia experience high caregiver burden (CB) and reduced quality of life (QoL), yet evidence on caregiver training remains limited.  To evaluate the effects of an online training program on caregivers’ QoL and CB.  A quasi-experimental pre–post study was conducted. Caregivers completed the WHOQOL-BREF and Zarit Scale at baseline and after a four-week training program.  Sixty-four caregivers completed the program; 42.1% reported clinically significant burden at baseline. Following the intervention, improvements in overall QoL ( p = 0.001) and reductions in CB ( p = 0.031) were observed among caregivers. These changes were greater among caregivers with baseline burden. Higher educational attainment was associated with increased odds of CB (OR = 1.243, 95% CI: 1.053–1.468).  Online caregiver training was associated with improved caregiver well-being and lower CB, supporting its potential integration into dementia care. However, the absence of a control group limits causal inference.

records.title: “I Wanted to Get Back Out There”: In-depth Interviews With Older Adults and Family Caregivers About Moving Out of Nursing Homes Using Medicaid’s Money Follows the Person Program and How Dementia Influences Transitions
records.abstract: Medicaid’s Money Follows the Person (MFP) Program enables nursing home residents to return to community living, yet people living with dementia (PLWD) less often transition to the community through MFP, for unclear reasons. To understand mechanisms underlying this disparity, we conducted in-depth interviews with 44 older adults in Connecticut eligible for MFP and 44 family caregivers (41% PLWD/PLWD family members). Desire to move, program awareness, ability to self-advocate, personal care needs, family support, housing and home and community-based services (HCBS) resources all influenced moves. PLWD less often desired to move, typically required more assistance to move, were less able to self-advocate and manage logistics, had higher personal care needs, needed more family/informal support, and had additional safety and supervision needs. Better support for PLWD is needed in transition and HCBS programs as the population grows, nursing homes beds decrease, and the desire to live in the community persists.

records.title: Residential context and cognitive aging: Differences by urbanicity across the retirement transition
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Cognitive aging is shaped by biological and social processes that unfold across the life course and the contexts in which they occur. Retirement may coincide with faster cognitive decline. Because cognitively supportive resources differ across places, this study assesses whether residential context (urban, suburban, rural/ex-urban) moderates cognitive trajectories before and after retirement.  Data were drawn from the U.S. Health and Retirement Study (2000-2020; n = 3,675). We estimated within-person change in cognition before and after retirement and included interaction terms to test modification by residential context. To reduce compositional differences across contexts, we applied inverse probability of treatment weighting and estimated piecewise linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes.  Cognitive decline was observed before and after retirement, with faster decline following retirement. Post-retirement decline was steepest in rural areas (-0.194 points/year), followed by suburban (-0.184) and urban (-0.164) settings. Pairwise contrasts indicated steeper post-retirement decline in rural than urban areas (β = -0.031 points/year), or 0.31 points over 10 years; urban-suburban differences were small.  were similar after combining urban and suburban respondents. Discussion Retirement may represent a turning point during which geographic inequalities in cognitive aging widen. Faster post-retirement decline in rural contexts may reflect reduced access to social, environmental, and institutional resources, but these pathways were not directly tested and should be interpreted as plausible explanations. Findings point to the potential importance of place-based strategies to mitigate spatial disparities in cognitive aging among retirees.

records.title: Changes in salivary oxytocin and subjective well-being in older women participating in direct or remote intergenerational exchange with children: a prospective observational study
records.abstract: This study examined changes in salivary oxytocin concentrations and subjective well-being accompanying direct and remote intergenerational exchange with children in older women. Given the increasing use of remote communication, we also examined whether similar physiological and psychological changes were observed in the remote condition.  We conducted a prospective observational cohort study among community-dwelling older women in Japan. Participants took part in either a direct face-to-face exchange or a remote exchange via video call. Saliva was collected at 10:00 (T1) and 11:00 (T2) on the reference day and at 11:00 on the exchange day (T4). The primary outcome was salivary oxytocin concentration, with the primary contrast defined as T4 relative to the same-clock-time T2 measurement on the reference day. Subjective well-being was assessed using the Personal Wellbeing Index (PWI) and a numerical rating scale (NRS) from T1 to T6 and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Sensitivity analyses were also performed.  Forty-six women enrolled; 40 were included in the final analysis (Direct, n = 18; Remote, n = 22). The geometric mean ratio (GMR) of salivary oxytocin at T4 relative to T2 was 1.220 (95% CI 0.987–1.507) in the Direct group and 1.046 (95% CI 0.851–1.284) in the Remote group. The ratio of GMRs for Direct versus Remote was 1.166 (95% CI 0.877–1.551), with no evidence of a between-group difference. PWI and NRS showed positive changes from immediately before to immediately after the exchange, but changes in the same direction were also observed on the reference day. Neither outcome showed a significant group-by-time interaction.  In the Direct group, salivary oxytocin at T4 was estimated to be higher than at the same-clock-time T2 measurement on the reference day, but the primary analysis was not statistically significant and there was no evidence of a between-group difference. Positive changes in subjective well-being around the exchange were also observed on the reference day and therefore could not be interpreted as exchange specific. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for same-clock-time reference-day measurements and non-specific study-context effects when evaluating short-term physiological and psychological changes accompanying intergenerational exchange.

records.title: Healthcare Provider Experiences Delivering Dementia Care in Indigenous Communities: Challenges and Recommendations
records.abstract: and  Little is known regarding the effects of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) in in American Indian and First Nation (AI/FN) communities in the US and Canada. Yet, research suggests FN populations in Canada experience 34% higher dementia rates and over half of US-based Indigenous adults demonstrate incident cognitive impairment, including dementia due to AD and/or cerebrovascular disease. Already higher than the general population, rates will increase as Indigenous populations age. The Indigenous Cultural Understandings of ADRD-Research and Engagement (ICARE) project was established to understand lived-experiences of dementia in AI/FN communities around the Great Lakes. We report themes describing practitioner experiences providing dementia care in selected US and Canadian Indigenous communities. Research Design and  Healthcare practitioners (n = 14) providing care in Indigenous communities were interviewed by community-based researchers using semi-structured guides exploring a range of topics. Thematic analysis was used to identify challenges and recommendations to improve care. Trustworthiness checks included reflexivity, consensus, prolonged engagement, member checking and audit.  Thematic analysis yielded six superordinate themes. Provider-perceived challenges included: 1) Limited Resources for Providing Dementia Care, 2) Need for Caregiver-focused Preparation and Support, 3) Communication and Relationship Gaps, 4) Low-levels of Community Dementia-related Awareness, Education and Engagement. Provider recommendations were characterized as: 5) Increase Dementia-related Awareness, Education and Engagement, 6) Invest in Dementia Caregiver Support and Community Strengths.  Findings were contextualized with post-colonial and relational care frameworks. Providers described relevant challenges and provided culturally safe and equitable strategies to improve dementia care outcomes.

records.title: Caregiver Perspectives on Alzheimer’s Care in the Turkish Sociocultural Context
records.abstract: In the context of global demographic change, the number of patients with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and other forms of dementia is steadily increasing. These individuals require ongoing care but often struggle to communicate their needs and preferences regarding quality care. This study re-examines existing qualitative data to explore perceptions of “quality care” for patients with AD within the Turkish sociocultural context. Building on a primary study of caregivers’ definitions of quality care, it employs a secondary analysis approach to generate new insights without collecting additional data. The dataset includes face-to-face, semi-structured interviews conducted in 2018 with 15 formal and informal caregivers, including family members, professional caregivers, and managers from care institutions across four provinces in Türkiye. Analysis reveals that patients with AD often experience discomfort when their bodies are exposed or touched, particularly in ways that infringe upon their sense of privacy. Caregivers emphasised that protecting privacy relies on understanding the individual’s life story, values, and preferences, highlighting the role of relational familiarity in delivering care. Many participants described forming close, family-like bonds, often adopting kinship roles to provide personalised support. These dynamics were also shaped by gender norms, with caregiving commonly framed through a mother-child lens, reflecting societal expectations that women assume primary caregiving responsibilities. The findings show how privacy, emotional closeness, and gender roles intersect to shape caregiving practices. These findings suggest that care quality for patients with AD in Türkiye may be enhanced by approaches that attend to cultural and relational dimensions, recognise caregiver support needs, and incorporate culturally attuned practices — though further research across diverse settings is needed to assess the broader applicability of these insights. These insights contribute to the international discourse on dementia care by showing how culturally specific practices can guide globally relevant approaches to quality care.

records.title: Linking Online Learning Time to Social Participation Among Older Adults: Urban-Rural Differences in the Online Learning Performance and Efficacy Pathways
records.abstract: Lifelong learning is known to promote social participation among older adults. However, in the digital age, it remains unclear whether online learning yields a positive effect and what the mechanisms are.  A total of 1,013 older adults aged 60 years and above completed the online learning efficacy scale, the online learning performance checklist, and the social participation checklist. Participants also self-reported their online learning time.  Online learning time was positively associated with social participation. The association was mediated by online learning efficacy and by a sequential pathway from online learning performance to online learning efficacy. These mediating effects were stronger among rural older adults than among urban older adults.  Active digital engagement among older adults may promote social participation, with particularly strong benefits for rural older adults. To promote active aging, future policies should incorporate internet-based learning programs into social participation interventions in rural areas.

records.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
records.abstract: The links between adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), intrinsic capacity (IC) trajectories in older adults and the role of social support remain unclear.  Using data from 3,897 Chinese adults aged 60 + years in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. IC was assessed at Waves 1 and 3. ACEs were from the Life Event Survey. Psychological capacity declines were associated with total ACEs (−0.024, 95% CI: −0.040, −0.008) and threat-related ACEs (−0.030, 95% CI: −0.052, −0.007). Social support did not mediate these associations.  ACEs are linked to domain-specific IC declines, modified by living arrangement.

records.title: Clinical Group Assignment in Home Health Care for Medicare Beneficiaries With ADRD: A 2019 Pre-PDGM Simulation
records.abstract: The Patient-Driven Groupings Model (PDGM) assigns home health episodes to clinical groups using primary diagnosis codes. The implications of this approach for beneficiaries with ADRD, whose condition is rarely coded as primary, are unclear.  To compare simulated PDGM clinical group assignment between ADRD-highly likely and ADRD-unlikely episodes.  Using national 2019 Medicare fee-for-service data, we simulated clinical group assignment and compared primary diagnosis profiles before and after 1:1 propensity score matching.  Nine in ten ADRD-highly likely episodes carried a non-ADRD primary diagnosis. After matching on demographics, comorbidity, and functional and cognitive status, clinical group assignment differences between cohorts attenuated but persisted. Most strikingly, ADRD-highly likely episodes were nearly 12 times as frequently assigned to Behavioral Health, the group with the lowest average payment weight, and comprised 92.1% of all matched Behavioral Health episodes. Within clinical groups, primary diagnosis profiles differed between cohorts, suggesting distinct care needs.

records.title: Changing care work and support needs across the home-based dementia care trajectory: a qualitative study of family caregivers in China
records.abstract: In China, most people living with dementia receive care at home from family members. Dementia caregiving changes over time, yet less is known about how caregivers’ support needs are reconfigured within ongoing home-based care as family responsibilities and interactions with health and care services change. This study explored how caregivers retrospectively described changes in caregiving responsibilities and associated support needs across the home-based dementia care trajectory.  This qualitative descriptive study involved 38 primary family caregivers in Guangzhou, China, who participated in face-to-face semi-structured interviews between February and December 2024. Participants were recruited using purposive maximum variation sampling, and data were analysed using the framework method. The identified phases were treated as analytically reconstructed and overlapping rather than fixed or linear.  Support needs did not simply increase over time but were reconfigured as family care work changed. Before formal help-seeking, caregivers had to interpret ambiguous changes, judge whether they warranted concern, and decide how to seek help. They therefore needed accessible risk-recognition information, clear entry points to assessment, and low-barrier, non-stigmatising routes to formal support. While engaging with services, caregiving shifted towards navigating pathways, coordinating across settings, maintaining continuity, and negotiating family decisions. Caregivers consequently needed clearer care pathways, continuity and handover support, service coordination, and family decision support. While sustaining care at home, the central challenge became maintaining everyday manageability amid repetitive tasks, symptom fluctuation, emotional strain, and financial pressure. Caregivers needed practical relief, actionable symptom-management guidance, emotional support, financial protection, and services compatible with family routines.  Caregivers’ support needs were shaped not only by dementia-related changes, but also by the reorganisation of family care work and encounters with fragmented services. These findings suggest that support may be more responsive when aligned with transitions in caregiving responsibilities and service engagement rather than with dementia severity alone.

records.title: Domain-Specific Associations of Physical Activity With Phase Angle and Extracellular Water–to–Total Body Water Ratio in Middle-Aged or Older Adults: Cross-Sectional Study
records.abstract: The phase angle (PhA) and extracellular water (ECW)–to–total body water (TBW) ratio serve as indicators of cell membrane integrity and body fluid balance in older adults.  This study examined the domain-specific associations of physical activity (PA) with PhA and the ECW-to-TBW ratio.  A nationally representative sample of 5211 adults aged 50 years and older was analyzed. Weekly amounts of moderate-to-vigorous PA (MVPA) in leisure-time, occupational, and transport-related domains were assessed using the Global Physical Activity Questionnaire. A bioelectrical impedance analyzer was used to measure PhA (°) and the ECW-to-TBW ratio (%). Linear regression analyses were conducted.  For leisure-time PA, compared with 0 min/week, participating in 150 to 299 min/week and ≥300 min/week of MVPA was associated with 0.08 (95% CI 0.02-0.14) and 0.13 (95% CI 0.06-0.20) degrees higher PhA, respectively. Additionally, compared with 0 min/week, engaging in 150 to 299 min/week and ≥300 min/week of MVPA was associated with –0.11 (95% CI –0.19 to –0.03) and –0.15 (95% CI –0.22 to –0.07) percentage points lower ECW-to-TBW ratio, respectively. For transport-related PA, compared with 0 min/week, engaging in ≥300 min/week of MVPA was negatively associated with the ECW-to-TBW ratio (β=–0.07, 95% CI –0.14 to –0.01). Occupational PA showed no clear associations with PhA or the ECW-to-TBW ratio.  While the observed associations were modest, the associations of PA with both PhA and the ECW-to-TBW ratio differed across PA domains. Specifically, leisure-time PA was positively associated with PhA and inversely associated with the ECW-to-TBW ratio. These findings highlight the potential role of leisure-time PA in improving bioelectrical markers of cellular health and fluid distribution.

records.title: Exploring Epigenetic Aging and Cognitive Change in Middle Adulthood
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Greater age deviation (AgeDev), in which a person’s biological age is older than their chronological age, is associated with worse cognitive performance. Most findings, however, rely on lab-administered cognitive measures and do not account for time-ordered effects of practice. The present study leveraged a measurement burst dataset to examine six distinct features of cognitive performance (peak performance, change in peak performance, intraindividual variability, forgetting, retest-related gains), and explored whether individual differences in these features can be predicted by AgeDev. In a sample of 139 adults aged 25-65, baseline AgeDev (Horvath1, Horvath2, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge), DunedinPACE, and SystemsAge were derived from DNA methylation. Across four annual high-frequency assessment bursts, processing speed and working memory were assessed via a Symbol Search and N-Back task, respectively. Using Bayesian Double Exponential Models (BDEMs), we found that baseline peak performance was lower for individuals with greater AgeDev, DunedinPACE, and chronological age. Interestingly, individuals with greater AgeDev and faster DunedinPACE showed greater retest-related gains within and across bursts. Neither AgeDev nor chronological age predicted differences in cognitive change across time. Individuals with greater AgeDev showed more intraindividual variability in processing speed. Finally, greater chronological age (but not AgeDev) was linked with more forgetting between bursts in both tasks. These findings underscore the value of multidimensional indices of cognitive performance. Importantly, even in a sample spanning young adulthood through early old age, such indices may provide unique information regarding the nature of longitudinal patterns in cognition associated with chronological or biological aging.

records.title: The 4 Ss Framework for Designing Age-Friendly Communities of the Future: Focus Group Study
records.abstract: Digital technology is increasingly being used to deliver interventions and initiatives to support the well-being of older adults. However, few studies have conducted needs assessments to identify the future well-being service requirements of an older adult population and their preferred modes of delivery, whether via digital technology or, in- person, or a combination of both (ie, a hybrid model).  This study aims to investigate the requirements of a rural region in New Zealand to inform planning to meet the future well-being needs of its older adult population over the next 30 years.  In total, 2 focus group discussions and 13 interviews were held with participants using a combination of phone and video calls. A total of 31 adults aged 61 years or older participated. The participants were asked how they saw the future well-being needs of the older adult population evolving, the role of digital technology and/or in-person interactions in delivering well-being services, and perceived barriers to, and enablers of, digital technology for providing services. Focus group and interview transcripts were thematically analyzed.  A total of 4 key well-being themes were identified across both focus group discussions and interviews with participants: —“services,” “support,” “spaces,” and “social connection,” —with an overarching finding that future age-friendly planning must prioritize social and community well-being outcomes, ensuring that investments in services, digital inclusion, and public spaces strengthen older adults’ ability to connect with others and participate fully in community life.  Digital technology is developing at a rapid pace, and as a result, we need to consider how to plan for the transition and bridge the gap identified between the current use of digital technology and its potential future use if technology is to support the older adults of the future. The findings indicate that older adults prefer to engage in- person, while trust is a barrier to digital technology use for some participants. The future offers many opportunities to support the well-being of older adults and communities through the application of the proposed 4 Ss Framework.

records.title: Life-course sociodemographic influences on mobility decline: a comparative qualitative study of older adults’ perspectives in Canada and Nigeria
records.abstract: Mobility is fundamental to healthy ageing and quality of life, as it enables older adults to continue participating in all spheres of life, including social, cultural, civic, spiritual, and economic activities. This study explored and compared the perspectives of Canadian and Nigerian older adults regarding life-course sociodemographic influences on mobility decline. The two distinct national contexts provided insight into mobility decline between high-income and low-resource settings shaped by unique cultural, economic, and policy environments.  We recruited eighteen Canadian and eighteen Nigerian community-dwelling older adults from diverse sociodemographic strata through community-based organisations. Using a qualitative description design, we interviewed the participants about their experiences with and observations about mobility decline. The transcripts were coded and analysed using conventional content analysis.  Of the 36 participants aged 65 to 89 years, 47.2% were women, 66.7% had a spouse or partner, and 86.1% were middle-income earners. We categorised findings into four domains: demographic, socioeconomic, sociocultural, and socioenvironmental factors. Demographic factors such as older age, ageism, women’s gender roles, and singlehood or widowhood were perceived to influence mobility decline among older adults negatively. However, most Canadian participants perceived no gender-related influence, highlighting the cultural differences in perspectives between the two groups. Socioeconomic factors (education, occupation type, and income), sociocultural factors (traditional dietary patterns, religious practices, and social participation), and socioenvironmental factors (urban versus rural living conditions, housing, and climatic challenges) were also perceived to influence the mobility trajectories of older adults. Most Canadians perceived poorer mobility among rural dwellers, while Nigerians believed the converse. We also documented the recommendations that participants made for mitigating mobility decline, including their advocacy for supportive environments and policies that recognise the unique sociodemographic contexts of older adults.  Sociodemographic factors may disproportionately influence mobility decline. Policymakers can enhance equity in ageing experiences by implementing age-friendly community initiatives that support the mobility of older adults, especially in low-resource and rural areas. records.title: Understanding the Care Priorities, Service Needs, and Lived Experiences of Rural Older Adults with Dementia and Cognitive Impairment in Canada: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: and  Research on dementia care remains largely urban-centric, with limited understanding about the lived experiences and needs of people with cognitive impairment and dementia in rural communities. This scoping review aimed to understand the care priorities, service needs, and lived experiences of rural older adults with cognitive impairment and dementia in Canada. Research Design and  Following Arksey and O’Malley’s scoping review framework, we searched CINAHL, PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science for journal articles published from January 2015 to January 2025. Two reviewers independently screened the articles and extracted data from the relevant articles. We used reflexive thematic analysis to analyze the data.  The scoping review identified 616 initial articles, with 16 relevant studies included in our review. Four interconnected themes were identified: i) complex navigational pathways and barriers in rural dementia care; ii) limited dementia knowledge creates challenges across the disease trajectory; iii) gaps in access to dementia-related services and supports; and iv) dementia-related stigma, fear, and social isolation. records.title: Rationale, Design, and Baseline Characteristics of the TARGET (Targeted Assessment and Recruitment of Geriatrics for Effective Fall Prevention Treatments) Cohort of Older Adults for Assessing Fall and Fracture Risk: Prospective Cohort Study
records.abstract: Falls and fractures are a major clinical concern for older adults. International clinical guidelines recommend annual fall risk screening for all adults aged 60 years and older. However, existing falls risk–screening algorithms have shown limited sensitivity and specificity in detecting future falls. Emerging health technologies, including wearable sensors, in-silico finite element models (FEMs), and virtual reality (VR) technology, show promise in enhancing fall and fracture risk assessments by providing more personalized  data to support targeted primary prevention. However, large-scale longitudinal studies are required to evaluate their predictive accuracy and cost-effectiveness for systematic community–based screening.  The TARGET (Targeted Assessment and Recruitment of Geriatrics for Effective Fall Prevention Treatments) study is an ongoing national prospective cohort study in Singapore designed to develop cost-effective and scalable frameworks for the early detection and prevention of falls and fractures using novel health technologies. This paper describes the rationale, design, and baseline characteristics of TARGET, and provides preliminary insights into how these novel technologies perform in discriminating between older adults with and with no history of falls at study baseline.  A total of 2291 community-dwelling Singapore residents aged ≥60 years were enrolled between 2022 and 2024. Participants underwent a comprehensive baseline fall risk assessment comprising (1) home-based interview to assess sociodemographic, anthropometric, cognitive, physical, functional, and psychosocial status; (2) gait assessment using wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) motion sensors; (3) dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry and whole-body 3D scans to construct subject-specific FEMs; and (4) VR-based cognitive assessment to probe spatial navigation deficits. Prospective follow-up for 2 years is ongoing, with linkage to national electronic medical records (EMRs) to obtain detailed clinical, medication, and pathological data.  Of the total cohort, 58% (1327/2291) were female, with a mean age of 74.6 years at baseline. TARGET represents a relatively healthy older adult population, with 83% (1898/2291) remaining fully independent, 44% (1016/2290) with mild cognitive impairment, 50% (440/879) with osteopenia, and 15% (358/2291) reporting falls in the past year. Significant baseline functional, psychosocial, cognitive, and biomechanical differences were identified between fallers and nonfallers. Fallers had poorer physical and psychosocial health, greater gait variability, and a higher risk of osteoporotic fractures. Novel risk prediction models integrating epidemiological, IMUs, FEM, VR, and EMR data are in development and being validated against gold standard clinical assessments, with cost-effectiveness evaluations of the economic feasibility of adopting these screening measures at scale.  Leveraging comprehensive epidemiological, EMR, and health technology data, TARGET is well positioned to identify novel biomarkers and systemic interactions that may predict falls and fracture risk, with potential application to other age-related diseases with shared pathophysiology. In particular, TARGET’s focus on community-based screening using technologies that can be administered by nonclinical personnel has the potential to reduce substantial burden and costs within the health care sector.

records.title: Workplace Violence in Home Health: Staff and Leadership Experiences and Strategies
records.abstract: and  Workplace violence (WPV) in healthcare has increased over the last decade, yet limited evidence exists to guide home health agency (HHA) prevention efforts. This study examined HHA leaders and staff WPV experiences, including the type of violence, risk factors, and prevention strategies. Research Design and  We conducted one-on-one semi-structured phone interviews with a purposive HHA sample of (a) 105 leaders, each representing a different organization, between November 2020-December 2022 and (b) 28 staff from five agencies between April 2023-August 2025. The socioecological framework guided the thematic analysis.  Leaders and staff contrasted the solitary, uncontrolled, and unpredictable HHA work environment with institutional healthcare contexts. HHA staff experiences reflected three types of WPV (i.e., criminal intent, violence perpetrated by the patient or others in the home, ideological violence perpetrated by the public). WPV risk factors spanned all domains of the socioecological framework. HHA staff and leaders described individual- and organizational-level WPV prevention strategies that targeted risk factors across framework domains. There was an absence of prevention strategies initiated at the community- and societal-level (e.g., WPV prevention legislation). Organizational strategies extended beyond annual staff training to include patient-specific safety plans, employing safety escorts, and discharge protocols for patient non-compliance with safety plans.  Fostering HHA staff safety within the context of service delivery is complex and multi-dimensional. Findings emphasized the importance of a comprehensive approach that is tailored to the HHA’s community and populations served and a need for societal-level policies addressing WPV prevention and mitigation.

records.title: Impact of supervised physical exercise on inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
records.abstract: and  Physical exercise is widely recognized as an effective non-pharmacological intervention that improves not only functional capacity, but also cognition and quality of life in older adults. However, the molecular pathways through which it influences aging-related processes remain incompletely understood. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesize current evidence on the effects of structured physical exercise intervention on molecular biomarkers associated with inflammation and oxidative stress in older adults. Research Design and  Randomized controlled trials which included participants ≥65 years old were identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Library.  A total of 50 reports (4,379 participants) were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 38 of them in the different meta-analyses performed. Exercise interventions ranged from 8 weeks to 12 months and included aerobic, resistance, and multicomponent training. Pooled analyses indicated modest but significant reductions in C-Reactive Protein (CRP) and high-sensitivity CRP, as well as increases in IL-10. Effects on other pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6 and TNF-α, were inconsistent across studies. Evidence from a limited number of trials (n = 6) also suggested improvements in redox balance.  Overall, structured physical exercise demonstrates a moderate immunomodulatory and antioxidant effect in older adults, although bias was moderate to high. PROSPERO registry: CRD420251006248.

records.title: Relationship Quality Trajectories and Financial Abuse Among Older Adults
records.abstract: and  Financial abuse is a prevalent yet underreported form of elder abuse with serious health and economic consequences. Prior research has linked poor relationship quality to financial abuse risk, but most studies rely on cross-sectional designs and focus on a single relationship type. This study examined whether 10-year changes in relationship quality with spouses, family, and friends are associated with subsequent financial abuse. Research Design and  Guided by social exchange theory, this study used data from three waves of the National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project. Relationship quality was categorized as stable, improving, or worsening over a 10-year period. Logistic regression models were estimated for each relationship type, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics.  Older adults with worsening family or friendship relationships over the 10-year period had more than twice the odds of experiencing subsequent financial abuse compared with those with stable relationships. Improving relationship trajectories were not significantly associated with financial abuse risk. Changes in spousal relationship quality were also not significantly associated with financial abuse.  These findings suggest that worsening family and friendship relationships over time may be an early indicator of financial abuse risk. Monitoring changes in older adults’ social relationships and supporting relationship stability may be important strategies for preventing financial abuse in later life.

records.title: Multimodal Dementia Prediction With Large Language Models: Cross-Attention Over Text, Audio, and Image
records.abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is a leading cause of dementia, and there is growing interest in scalable approaches for early screening using speech-based tasks. While prior work has demonstrated promising  using either transcript-based language features or acoustic cues, most approaches remain unimodal or rely on simple fusion strategies that do not explicitly consider interactions across modalities.  In this study, we propose an attention-based trimodal fusion framework that integrates text, audio, and image representations of the Cookie Theft picture, which serves as the shared visual stimulus in the picture-description task.  Our method uses a new bidirectional cross-attention mechanism to achieve a unified multimodal embedding for downstream tasks. We evaluate the approach on 2 tasks: AD detection by classifying whether the participant has AD or not, and AD severity assessment by predicting Mini-Mental Status Examination cognitive scores.  On the AD detection task, trimodal fusion achieves the best overall performance ( F 1 -score=0.8667, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve=0.9032), outperforming unimodal baselines, bimodal fusion, and conventional early or late fusion . For AD severity assessment, the proposed multimodal representation reduces prediction error of root mean squared error to about 4.20, improving over both unimodal and bimodal fusion settings. We further perform the ablation analysis to show that bidirectional cross-attention consistently outperforms conventional unidirectional cross-attention.  These  demonstrate that attention-based multimodal fusion can enhance dementia prediction from picture-description responses and provide a strong foundation for developing multimodal cognitive screening pipelines.

records.title: Tailored personas for home-based fall prevention among older adults with stroke: A qualitative study
records.abstract: and  Existing home-based fall prevention strategies often adopt a one-size-fits-all approach despite substantial heterogeneity among older adults with stroke. Persona-based  may facilitate more individualized intervention design, yet remain largely unexplored in stroke rehabilitation. This study explored variations in fall prevention self-management among older adults with stroke and developed user personas to represent their diverse experiences, challenges, and support needs. Research Design and  A qualitative descriptive study was conducted among 26 older adults with stroke receiving home-based care in China. Participants were recruited using purposive maximum-variation sampling. Semi-structured interviews were conducted between January and March 2026. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis to identify key dimensions of fall prevention self-management. Individual participant profiles were iteratively synthesized through cross-case comparison into composite personas representing recurring configurations of behaviors, beliefs, barriers, resources, and support needs.  Five distinct personas emerged: proactive self-managers, risk-discounting managers, routine-based managers, support-constrained managers, and professionally supported managers. These personas demonstrated distinct combinations of fall-risk perception, social resources, environmental constraints, and healthcare dependence.  The findings demonstrate substantial diversity in how older adults with stroke manage fall prevention in home settings. Persona-based stratification provides an actionable approach for designing scalable, context-sensitive fall prevention interventions.

records.abstract: and  Older adults often face significant barriers to mental health help-seeking. This study integrated participatory co-design with behavioural science principles to develop culturally meaningful hybrid nudges to normalise mental health help-seeking among older adults in Hong Kong. The embedded process evaluation highlighted perceived learning, ownership, and collaboration, as well as challenges such as self-doubt.  Participatory co-design can support the development of theory-informed and culturally attuned hybrid nudges to address motivational barriers to mental health help-seeking. Future research should test acceptability and behavioural outcomes through randomized or pragmatic trials, and examine how to balance theoretical fidelity with participant agency in co-designed behavioural interventions.

records.title: Atypical survey response patterns as early indicators of dementia onset: A coordinated analysis across longitudinal aging cohorts
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Atypical survey response patterns, such as inconsistent or implausible responses, have been linked to lower cognitive functioning in later life. This study examined whether these behaviors predict future dementia onset across diverse longitudinal studies of aging.  We conducted a coordinated analysis of data from eight longitudinal studies of aging (total N = 76,350). We derived five common types of atypical response pattern indicators from participants’ questionnaire data. Associations with subsequent dementia risk were examined within each cohort using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for demographic covariates and accounting for death as a competing risk.  were synthesized using random-effects meta-analysis .  Across cohorts, significant associations with incident dementia were observed for item-nonresponse (overall hazard ratio [HR] per SD increase = 1.06), random response errors (HR = 1.25), multivariate outlier responses (HR = 1.31), and incompatible response patterns indexed by Guttman errors and person-fit statistics (HRs = 1.22–1.25). Extreme responding was not significantly associated with dementia risk. Secondary analyses suggested stronger associations among individuals younger than 75 years and those with higher levels of education. Discussion Routine survey responses contain behavioral signals associated with emerging dementia risk. Because these indicators can be derived from existing survey data without additional testing burden, they may provide a scalable complement to traditional approaches for studying cognitive aging in large population-based cohorts.

records.title: Adiposity and Cognitive Performance in Older Men and Women from the Study of Muscle, Mobility and Aging (SOMMA)
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Aging is accompanied by changes in body composition and cognition. Although adiposity has been linked to metabolic dysfunction and dementia risk, associations with specific cognitive domains in later life remain unclear.  This cross-sectional study examined associations between adiposity and cognitive performance in 769 community-dwelling, healthy older adults (70–94 years) from the Study of Muscle, Mobility and Aging (SOMMA). Adiposity was assessed using anthropometric measures (body mass index, waist circumference) and MRI-derived regional fat volumes, including visceral and abdominal subcutaneous adipose tissue. Cognitive performance was evaluated using a screening measure (Montreal Cognitive Assessment), processing speed (Digit Symbol Coding Test), executive function (Trail Making Test B), and memory (California Verbal Learning Test–II Short Form). Multivariable linear regression models were sequentially adjusted for demographic, cardiometabolic, psychosocial, and behavioral factors.  Greater age was associated with lower adiposity and poorer cognitive performance (p  In healthy older adults, adiposity is most consistently related to processing speed, whereas associations with memory and executive function are weaker or absent. Processing speed may be especially sensitive to adiposity-related differences. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal relationships.

records.title: Associations between social network characteristics and daily social experiences in later life: Evidence from ecological momentary assessment
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Sociological theory posits that social networks function as enduring relational structures that constrain and enable everyday social interactions, yet empirical evidence linking network properties to real-time social exposures remains limited. To address this gap, this study examines how older adults' social networks are associated with their daily social experiences.  Using data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas (SECHURA) study, we combine egocentric network data (1,474 alters from 254 respondents) with ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data capturing real-time social interactions over one week (5,342 observations). We evaluate associations between three network properties–structure (quantity, composition, and interconnectedness of network members), heterogeneity (diversity in gender, race/ethnicity, and age), and strength (strong and supportive ties) – and four momentary outcomes (number and type of interaction partners, social activities, and being outside the home).  Random-effects models show that larger and more socially diverse networks are associated with greater momentary social engagement, including more interaction partners, less time alone, and more explicit socializing. Both role diversity and network density are associated with heightened social exposure, through distinct pathways. Sociodemographic heterogeneity also predicts interaction patterns, with age heterogeneity linked to kin-centered interactions and racial heterogeneity to non-kin exposure. Stronger affective ties predicted less engagement in explicit socializing. Discussion Personal social networks operate as critical structures linked to the quantity, composition, and context of older adults' real-time social exposures. Large, densely connected, and role-diverse networks appear to facilitate everyday interactions through different mechanisms.

records.title: The role of gender in informant reports of cognitive decline in the United States and Mexico
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: This study investigates the influence of respondents’ and informants’ gender on informants’ assessments of cognitive functioning in population studies in the United States and Mexico.  Using data from the Harmonized Cognitive Assessment Protocol (HCAP) of the Health and Retirement Study (HRS-HCAP) (N = 3,025) in the United States and the Mexican Cognitive Aging Study (Mex-Cog) (N = 1071) in Mexico, we examined informant reports of cognitive decline with 17 questions from the Community Screening Instrument for Dementia (CSI-D). Ordinary least squares regression was used to analyze the gender of respondents and informants in each country for the total CSI-D score and logistic regressions for each individual CSI-D question, controlling for correlates of direct and informant measures of cognition.  There was no significant relationship between respondents’ gender and total CSI-D reports in either country. Female informants in the United States reported 0.57 more CSI-D symptoms compared to male informants while in Mexico they reported 1.35 fewer symptoms. Discussion Our  show that informant gender is associated with systematically different reporting patterns depending on the national and cultural context in which the assessment takes place. The  suggest that informant reports of cognitive decline may represent social norms in addition to actual cognitive decline.

records.title: There must be fifty ways to reduce ageism: A theoretical perspective on possible interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism among older persons
records.abstract: Ageism is defined as stereotypes, prejudices, and discrimination toward people because of their age. It represents a substantial public health concern given its high prevalence and extensive impact on the health and well-being of older persons. Although interventions to reduce ageism toward older persons among younger persons as agents of ageism exist, much less is known about interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism toward older persons among older persons. This theoretical paper addresses the gap by proposing a comprehensive framework for the development of interventions to reduce ageism among older persons in the second half of life. Drawing on established theories, such as contact theory, terror management theory, stereotype embodiment theory, and social identity theory, we propose various mechanisms through which ageism among older persons can be reduced. The paper explores theoretical assumptions about which interventions work for whom and why to guide further empirical research on the reduction of ageism in the second half of life. We argue that although at the present time, effective interventions to reduce ageism among older persons are scarce, there are many theoretical avenues that may prove effective.

records.title: Development and Validation of the Attitudes Toward Healthcare Providers (ATHP) Scale: A Three-Study Investigation of Perceived Interpersonal and Institutional Ageism in Clinical Care
records.abstract: and  Ageism in healthcare contributes to undertreatment, dismissive communication, and age-based exclusions from care, yet no psychometrically validated, patient-reported measure captures older adults’ perceptions of age-based bias during clinical encounters. We developed and validated the Attitudes Toward Healthcare Providers (ATHP) scale. Research Design and  Items adapted from four validated discrimination measures plus two new items were administered to community-dwelling adults aged 65 and older in three independent, predominantly non-Hispanic White samples (Ns = 223, 349, 361) recruited through Prolific within the United States. Study 1 examined latent structure with exploratory factor analysis; Study 2 tested and refined the structure with confirmatory factor analysis; Study 3 confirmed the refined model and evaluated reliability, measurement invariance across gender, and construct validity.  Study 1 identified two correlated factors, Interpersonal and Institutional Ageism, corroborated by parallel analysis and Velicer’s MAP test. Study 2 indicated that a 20-item model fit poorly and that removing three items produced a refined 17-item model. Study 3 confirmed this model (CFI = .926, RMSEA = .058, SRMR = .057), with excellent reliability for Interpersonal Ageism and the total scale, good reliability for Institutional Ageism, full scalar invariance across gender, and coherent discriminant and convergent validity.  The 17-item ATHP is a psychometrically sound, healthcare-specific measure distinguishing interpersonal from institutional ageism, equipping researchers, health systems, and policymakers to monitor age-based bias and evaluate interventions.

records.abstract: This study examines how life expectancy (LE) without and with depression differs by living arrangement among older adults in Japan, with particular attention to gender differences. records.title: Bridge jobs and retirement identities: Gendered life course approach to workforce exits among Early Boomers
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: The prevalence of bridge jobs, post-career work that bridges between career jobs and workforce exit, has obfuscated the isomorphic link between older adults’ role identities as retirees, named ‘retirement identities’, and their actual labor force status in ways that may well differ by gender. We examine how gender and Social Security eligibility/receipt are associated with retirement identities, and how these identities are associated with the timing of final workforce exit.  We track bridge job take-ups and workforce exits of Early Boomers (ages 51-56 in 2004, N = 910) in the Health and Retirement Study 2004-2020. We use multinomial logistic regression to examine predictors of retirement identities by gender, and event history analysis to examine the timing of workforce exit at the intersection of gender, retirement identity, and timing of bridge job take-up.  Findings reveal that Social Security receipt is associated with men’s retirement identity formation, but not women’s. For both genders, ordered retirement identities, from ‘not retired’ to ‘completely retired,’ predict the timing of workforce exits. Women in bridge jobs do not always exit the workforce earlier than men when retirement identities are taken into account. Discussion This study underscores the changes in retirement as an institutionalized and gendered life course status passage, amplified by the increasing pivoting to bridge jobs, but with considerable variability in self-definitions of retirement status. Our evidence suggests that these identities serve as good signals of older workers’ work attachments and retirement plans, offering helpful insights for policymakers and employers.
